title: Cardiology
rationale: Requested module, aimed at the Cardiology gaps the tracker actually shows. STEMI reperfusion is 0% — the miss was transferring for primary PCI when the centre was 150 minutes away, and dropping the anticoagulant from the fibrinolysis package. Myocarditis is 0%. RV infarct versus posterior MI has sat open since 14 August as an unresolved discrimination. Perioperative anticoagulation and bridging are deliberately excluded here because the Anticoagulation module already teaches them.
objectives: Choose between primary PCI and fibrinolysis in STEMI using the time-to-PCI rule, and state the full drug package that accompanies each.
Recognise right ventricular infarction from an inferior STEMI and explain why nitrates are withheld.
Separate myocarditis from acute rheumatic fever and from ACS in a young patient with chest pain.
Build heart failure treatment from ejection fraction, and name what changes in HFpEF.
Decide rate versus rhythm control in atrial fibrillation, and recognise when immediate cardioversion is required.

sections.heading: STEMI — the 120-minute rule and the whole package
sections.body:
Two decisions, and the second is the one that gets dropped.

**Decision 1 — which reperfusion.** The threshold is **time from first medical contact to balloon**:

| Time to PCI | Strategy |
|---|---|
| **≤120 minutes** | **Primary PCI** |
| **>120 minutes** | **Fibrinolysis now**, then transfer for angiography within 3–24 h |

A centre 150 minutes away is **outside** the window. Transferring anyway and accepting a 2.5-hour delay to reperfusion is the classic error: lysing locally and *then* transferring beats a long transfer for PCI.

**Decision 2 — what goes with it.** Fibrinolysis is never a single drug:

| | Give |
|---|---|
| **Primary PCI** | Aspirin 300 mg + a P2Y12 inhibitor (ticagrelor or prasugrel) + procedural anticoagulation |
| **Fibrinolysis** | **Tenecteplase** + aspirin + **clopidogrel** + an **anticoagulant** (enoxaparin, or heparin) |

**The anticoagulant is the part most often forgotten**, and omitting it raises reinfarction. Note also that clopidogrel — not ticagrelor or prasugrel — is the P2Y12 agent paired with lysis, since the more potent agents were not studied with fibrinolytics and raise bleeding.

**Rescue PCI** if there is failed reperfusion at 60–90 minutes: ongoing pain, or less than 50% resolution of ST elevation.

**Absolute contraindications to fibrinolysis**: any prior intracranial haemorrhage, ischaemic stroke within 6 months, known cerebral vascular malformation or intracranial tumour, active bleeding, suspected aortic dissection, recent major trauma, surgery or head injury within 3 weeks.
sections.note: PCI within 120 minutes of first medical contact, otherwise lyse then transfer — and fibrinolysis means tenecteplase plus aspirin plus clopidogrel plus an anticoagulant.

sections.heading: Inferior STEMI — the right ventricle and the posterior wall
sections.body:
An inferior STEMI (II, III, aVF) prompts **two extra leads**, because two things hide behind it.

**Right ventricular infarction.** Suspect it whenever inferior ST elevation is bigger in **III than II**, or there is hypotension with **clear lung fields and a raised JVP**. Confirm with **right-sided leads — ST elevation in V4R**.

The consequence is a management reversal: the failing RV is **preload dependent**, so it needs volume and cannot tolerate anything that drops filling. **Nitrates, and equally opiates and diuretics, are withheld** — GTN in RV infarction can cause profound hypotension and arrest. Treat instead with **IV fluid loading**, then inotropes if fluid alone is insufficient.

**Posterior infarction.** Suspect it from **tall R waves and ST depression in V1–V3** — a mirror image, because no anterior lead faces the posterior wall. Confirm with **posterior leads V7–V9**, where you will see the true ST elevation. Posterior MI is a STEMI equivalent and needs reperfusion.

**Do not merge the two.** They often coexist and both arise from the right coronary or circumflex territory, but the exam point is separate: **posterior MI does not itself contraindicate GTN — RV infarction does**. Withholding nitrates is a response to RV involvement, and the trigger for that is V4R, not V7–V9.

Inferior MI also carries **bradyarrhythmias and heart block** through the AV nodal artery, which is usually transient and atropine-responsive.
sections.note: Inferior STEMI: get V4R and V7–V9. RV infarction is preload dependent so nitrates are withheld and fluid is given; posterior MI is a reperfusion decision, not a nitrate one.

sections.heading: Myocarditis — and what it is mistaken for
sections.body:
**Myocarditis** is new cardiac dysfunction after a viral prodrome, most often in a **young patient** where coronary disease is improbable.

The picture: coryzal or diarrhoeal illness one to two weeks earlier, then **chest pain, breathlessness, palpitations**, with signs of new heart failure — **raised JVP, third heart sound, functional mitral regurgitation** from ventricular dilatation. Troponin is raised, ECG shows non-specific ST/T change or **widespread saddle-shaped ST elevation with PR depression** if the pericardium is involved, and echo shows global hypokinesis. Cardiac MRI is the non-invasive confirmatory test.

| Confused with | How to exclude it |
|---|---|
| **Acute rheumatic fever** | ARF needs **Jones criteria including serological proof of preceding group A strep** — negative ASOT and anti-DNase B with carditis alone rules it out |
| **ACS** | Young, viral prodrome, **global** rather than territorial wall motion abnormality, unobstructed coronaries |
| **Pericarditis** | Pain relieved sitting forward, rub, **preserved** ventricular function — myocarditis has the dysfunction |

**Management is supportive**: standard heart failure therapy, and **avoid exercise** for 3–6 months because exertion during active myocarditis is associated with sudden death. **NSAIDs are avoided** where there is ventricular dysfunction. Most recover; a minority progress to dilated cardiomyopathy.
sections.note: New heart failure after a viral illness in a young patient is myocarditis; acute rheumatic fever cannot be diagnosed without serological evidence of preceding strep.

sections.heading: Heart failure — build it from the ejection fraction
sections.body:
**HFrEF (EF ≤40%)** has four drug classes that each independently reduce mortality — the **four pillars**, started early and together rather than sequentially:

| Pillar | Agent |
|---|---|
| RAAS | **ARNI** (sacubitril/valsartan) preferred over ACE inhibitor; ARB if intolerant |
| Beta blocker | Bisoprolol, carvedilol, metoprolol succinate |
| MRA | Spironolactone, eplerenone |
| **SGLT2 inhibitor** | Dapagliflozin, empagliflozin — **regardless of diabetes** |

**Diuretics treat symptoms, not mortality** — frusemide makes people feel better and changes no outcome, which is why it is not a pillar.

**HFpEF (EF ≥50%)** is the one where most of that evidence evaporates. **SGLT2 inhibitors are the exception**: they reduce hospitalisation and cardiovascular death in HFpEF, and are the only class with convincing benefit. Otherwise: diuretics for congestion, and aggressive treatment of the drivers — hypertension, atrial fibrillation, obesity, sleep apnoea.

**Devices in HFrEF**: an **ICD** for primary prevention where EF stays ≤35% despite optimal therapy; **CRT** where there is left bundle branch block with QRS ≥150 ms.

**Do not start a beta blocker in acute decompensation** — it is a therapy for the stable, euvolaemic patient, and starting it in pulmonary oedema worsens output.
sections.note: HFrEF gets all four pillars including an SGLT2 inhibitor regardless of diabetes; in HFpEF the SGLT2 inhibitor is the one class that still works.

sections.heading: Atrial fibrillation — rate, rhythm, or shock now
sections.body:
The first question is not rate versus rhythm. It is **is the patient unstable?**

**Immediate synchronised DC cardioversion** if AF is causing any of: **hypotension/shock, ischaemic chest pain, acute heart failure, or syncope**. Haemodynamic instability overrides every other consideration, including anticoagulation status.

If stable, the **48-hour rule** governs cardioversion:

| Onset | Approach |
|---|---|
| **<48 h**, no high-risk features | Cardiovert (electrical or chemical) with anticoagulation started |
| **>48 h or unknown** | Either **3 weeks of therapeutic anticoagulation** first, or a **TOE** to exclude atrial thrombus — then cardiovert, and anticoagulate for at least 4 weeks after either way |

Cardioverting an unanticoagulated patient in AF of uncertain duration risks embolising an established atrial thrombus.

**Rate versus rhythm for the long term**: rate control with a beta blocker or a non-dihydropyridine calcium channel blocker suits older, minimally symptomatic patients. Rhythm control (antiarrhythmic or ablation) is favoured in younger patients, persistent symptoms despite rate control, or heart failure — where early rhythm control improves outcomes.

**Anticoagulation is decided separately from both**, by **CHA₂DS₂-VASc**, and is unaffected by whether sinus rhythm is restored — a patient who cardioverts successfully still carries their stroke risk.

**Avoid verapamil, diltiazem and digoxin in AF with pre-excitation (WPW)**: blocking the AV node pushes conduction down the accessory pathway and can precipitate VF.
sections.note: Instability means immediate cardioversion; beyond 48 hours anticoagulate for 3 weeks or do a TOE first, and CHA₂DS₂-VASc decides anticoagulation independently of rhythm.

questions.stem: A 58-year-old man has an inferior STEMI diagnosed by paramedics in a rural town. Symptom onset was 90 minutes ago. The nearest PCI-capable centre is a 145-minute road transfer. He has no bleeding history, no prior stroke and BP is 132/78.
questions.lead: What is the most appropriate reperfusion strategy?
options: Aspirin and heparin alone, then transfer for primary PCI
Tenecteplase alone, with antiplatelets withheld until angiography
Aspirin, ticagrelor and enoxaparin, then transfer for rescue PCI if pain persists
Aspirin, ticagrelor and immediate transfer for primary PCI
Aspirin, clopidogrel, enoxaparin and tenecteplase now, then transfer for angiography
questions.explanation: Time from first medical contact to balloon would be well over 120 minutes, so the strategy is fibrinolysis now, then transfer for angiography within 3–24 hours — not a long transfer for primary PCI. The package matters as much as the decision: tenecteplase goes with aspirin, clopidogrel and an anticoagulant (enoxaparin). Omitting the anticoagulant raises reinfarction and is the commonest incomplete answer. Ticagrelor is the wrong P2Y12 agent alongside lysis — clopidogrel is the one studied with fibrinolytics.
questions.point: PCI beyond 120 minutes means lyse then transfer, and fibrinolysis is tenecteplase plus aspirin plus clopidogrel plus an anticoagulant.

questions.stem: A 64-year-old man has an inferior STEMI with ST elevation greater in lead III than lead II. BP is 84/56, HR 58. The chest is clear on auscultation and the JVP is elevated. He is given sublingual GTN for ongoing pain and becomes profoundly hypotensive.
questions.lead: What explains the deterioration, and what is the correct management?
options: Posterior extension — obtain posterior leads V7–V9 and reperfuse
Cardiogenic shock from LV failure — start an inotrope and give frusemide
Right ventricular infarction — give an IV fluid bolus and withhold further nitrates
Vasovagal response — lie the patient flat and repeat the GTN at a lower dose
Complete heart block — give atropine and prepare for pacing
questions.explanation: Inferior STEMI with elevation greater in III than II, hypotension, clear lungs and a raised JVP is right ventricular infarction — confirmed by ST elevation in V4R. The failing RV is preload dependent, so GTN, opiates and diuretics all drop filling and can cause collapse. Treatment is fluid loading, then inotropes if needed. Frusemide would compound the problem. Posterior infarction is a real and commonly coexisting finding, but it is a reperfusion question — it is RV involvement, not posterior involvement, that contraindicates nitrates.
questions.point: RV infarction is preload dependent: withhold nitrates, opiates and diuretics, and give fluid. Posterior MI does not itself contraindicate GTN.

questions.stem: A 24-year-old man presents with 3 days of chest pain, breathlessness on exertion and palpitations. He had a coryzal illness 10 days ago. HR 108, BP 106/64, JVP elevated, third heart sound and a soft pansystolic murmur at the apex. Troponin 890 ng/L. ECG shows widespread non-specific T wave changes. Echo shows global hypokinesis with EF 38%. ASOT and anti-DNase B are negative.
questions.lead: What is the most likely diagnosis?
options: Myocarditis
Acute pericarditis
Acute rheumatic fever
Acute coronary syndrome
Infective endocarditis
questions.explanation: New heart failure — raised JVP, S3, functional mitral regurgitation from ventricular dilatation — with a raised troponin and global hypokinesis in a young patient after a viral illness is myocarditis. Acute rheumatic fever requires Jones criteria including serological evidence of preceding group A streptococcal infection: negative ASOT and anti-DNase B with carditis alone excludes it, which is the specific trap here. ACS would give a territorial wall motion abnormality in a patient with plausible coronary risk. Pericarditis preserves ventricular function. Management is supportive with heart failure therapy, and exercise restriction for 3–6 months.
questions.point: Acute rheumatic fever cannot be diagnosed without serological proof of preceding strep — carditis after a viral illness with negative titres is myocarditis.

questions.stem: A 67-year-old man has HFrEF with EF 30%. He is euvolaemic on frusemide, and already established on sacubitril/valsartan, bisoprolol and spironolactone at target doses. He does not have diabetes. eGFR 62 mL/min. He remains NYHA class II.
options: Ivabradine
A higher dose of frusemide
Amiodarone
Digoxin
An SGLT2 inhibitor such as dapagliflozin
questions.explanation: The fourth pillar is an SGLT2 inhibitor, and its mortality and hospitalisation benefit in HFrEF is independent of diabetes status — the absence of diabetes in the stem is there to test exactly that. Increasing frusemide in a euvolaemic patient treats nothing: diuretics relieve congestion and do not change mortality. Ivabradine is considered only if the heart rate remains ≥70 in sinus rhythm on a maximally tolerated beta blocker. Digoxin reduces hospitalisation but not mortality and sits well down the list. Amiodarone has no mortality benefit in heart failure.
questions.point: SGLT2 inhibitors are a mortality pillar in HFrEF regardless of diabetes; diuretics are symptomatic only.

questions.stem: A 72-year-old woman presents with palpitations. ECG shows atrial fibrillation at 148 bpm. She reports the palpitations began "a few weeks ago, on and off". BP is 138/82, she has no chest pain, clear lungs and is comfortable at rest. She takes no anticoagulant.
questions.lead: What is the most appropriate management?
options: Digoxin loading and discharge with outpatient follow-up
Immediate synchronised DC cardioversion
Immediate chemical cardioversion with flecainide
Rate control and anticoagulation, with cardioversion deferred pending 3 weeks of anticoagulation or a TOE
Rate control alone, with anticoagulation decided after echocardiography
questions.explanation: She is haemodynamically stable, so nothing needs to happen immediately — and the AF has been present for more than 48 hours, so cardioverting now risks embolising an established atrial thrombus. The correct path is rate control plus anticoagulation, with cardioversion after either 3 weeks of therapeutic anticoagulation or a TOE excluding thrombus, followed by at least 4 weeks of anticoagulation afterwards. Immediate cardioversion is reserved for instability: hypotension, ischaemic pain, acute heart failure or syncope. Anticoagulation is decided by CHA₂DS₂-VASc, not by echo findings.
questions.point: Beyond 48 hours or unknown duration, cardioversion waits for 3 weeks of anticoagulation or a TOE — unless the patient is unstable.

questions.stem: A 26-year-old man presents with a rapid irregular tachycardia at 210 bpm with varying QRS morphology. His baseline ECG from last year shows a short PR interval and a delta wave. BP is 118/70 and he is alert.
options: Flecainide
Magnesium sulfate
Procainamide
Verapamil
Amiodarone
questions.explanation: The baseline delta wave and short PR indicate Wolff–Parkinson–White, and this is pre-excited atrial fibrillation. AV nodal blocking drugs — verapamil, diltiazem, digoxin, adenosine and beta blockers — are contraindicated: blocking the node diverts conduction down the accessory pathway, accelerating the ventricular rate and potentially precipitating ventricular fibrillation. Procainamide (or flecainide) acts on the accessory pathway and is the appropriate pharmacological choice, with DC cardioversion for any instability.
questions.point: In pre-excited AF, AV nodal blockers can precipitate VF — use procainamide or flecainide, or cardiovert.

questions.stem: A 55-year-old man is 90 minutes into treatment for an anterior STEMI with tenecteplase in a rural hospital. He still has chest pain, and the ST elevation in V2–V4 has reduced by only about 20% compared with the pre-treatment ECG.
questions.lead: What does this indicate and what should happen?
options: Failed reperfusion — repeat the dose of tenecteplase
Failed reperfusion — arrange urgent transfer for rescue PCI
Reperfusion arrhythmia — observe and repeat the ECG in 2 hours
Pericarditis — commence colchicine and an NSAID
Successful reperfusion — continue medical therapy and transfer routinely
questions.explanation: Successful reperfusion is judged at 60–90 minutes by resolution of pain and ≥50% reduction in ST elevation. Ongoing pain with only 20% resolution is failed fibrinolysis, and the answer is urgent transfer for rescue PCI — the delay that made lysis the right initial choice does not make PCI the wrong rescue. Repeating the lytic is not done: it adds bleeding risk without benefit. NSAIDs in early infarction impair healing and increase the risk of myocardial rupture.
questions.point: Assess reperfusion at 60–90 minutes: ongoing pain or under 50% ST resolution means failed lysis and rescue PCI.

questions.stem: A 78-year-old woman has HFpEF with EF 58%. She has hypertension, obesity and permanent atrial fibrillation. She is breathless on exertion with mild ankle oedema, and is already on frusemide and an anticoagulant.
questions.lead: Which additional treatment has the best evidence for reducing hospitalisation?
options: Digoxin
An SGLT2 inhibitor
Spironolactone
Sacubitril/valsartan
Bisoprolol
questions.explanation: Most HFrEF therapy does not transfer to HFpEF, where trials of ARNI, beta blockers and MRAs have been largely neutral. SGLT2 inhibitors are the exception — they reduce heart failure hospitalisation and cardiovascular death across the ejection fraction range, and are the class to add. Beyond that, HFpEF management is aggressive treatment of the drivers: blood pressure, atrial fibrillation, obesity and sleep apnoea, with diuretics for congestion alone.
questions.point: SGLT2 inhibitors are the one drug class with convincing benefit in HFpEF; the other HFrEF pillars do not transfer.

questions.stem: A 61-year-old man presents with chest pain. ECG shows ST depression of 2 mm in V1–V3 with tall R waves in V2, and upright T waves in those leads. Troponin is rising. There is no ST elevation in the limb leads.
questions.lead: What is the most appropriate next step?
options: Commence thrombolysis on the basis of the anterior ST depression
Treat as NSTEMI with medical therapy and inpatient angiography within 72 hours
Record posterior leads V7–V9 and, if ST elevation is present, treat as STEMI
Record right-sided leads V4R and give a fluid bolus
Repeat the ECG in 6 hours before making any decision
questions.explanation: ST depression with tall R waves in V1–V3 is the mirror image of posterior ST elevation — no standard lead faces the posterior wall, so the finding appears reversed anteriorly. The step is to record posterior leads V7–V9; ST elevation there confirms a posterior STEMI, which is a STEMI equivalent requiring immediate reperfusion. Treating it as an NSTEMI with routine timing is the error, since it delays reperfusion in a patient who needs it now. V4R answers a different question — right ventricular involvement in inferior infarction.
questions.point: ST depression with tall R waves in V1–V3 is posterior STEMI in disguise — record V7–V9 and reperfuse.

questions.stem: A 48-year-old man is admitted with acute pulmonary oedema on a background of newly diagnosed HFrEF (EF 25%). He is dyspnoeic at rest with crackles to the mid-zones, BP 104/68, HR 112.
questions.lead: Which treatment should NOT be commenced now?
options: Bisoprolol
An SGLT2 inhibitor once stabilised
Non-invasive ventilation if hypoxaemic despite oxygen
An ACE inhibitor once haemodynamically stable
IV frusemide
questions.explanation: Beta blockers are not started during acute decompensation. Their negative inotropic effect worsens output in a congested, poorly perfused patient; they are commenced once the patient is stable and euvolaemic, and if already established are usually continued at a reduced dose rather than stopped outright. IV frusemide and non-invasive ventilation are appropriate acute measures, and the disease-modifying agents are layered in as the patient stabilises. The distinction is between drugs that treat congestion now and drugs that change the trajectory later.
questions.point: Never start a beta blocker in acute decompensated heart failure — stabilise and achieve euvolaemia first.
